#216778. Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2680 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer.
  • I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.
  • Hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer. “Look at all the tracks you’ll see with snow covering the ground,” they chorus.

I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.

Hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are. And tracks may not necessarily indicate where deer are likely to be again. One deer can make a lot of tracks.

But if you know how snowfall changes a whitetail’s daily routine, you are starting to understand where you will find tracks — and the deer that made them.

Let’s rehearse some basic facts.

Recent findings suggest that first, snow normally comes late in most states’ deer seasons. That means whitetails already have been harassed by other hunters. Unless you hunt private land, all deer you are likely to encounter may be wary, even downright spooky. They are moving little during daylight hours. Rutting bucks are probably limiting much of their roaming to the darkness of night.

In a recent development, second, snowstorms — and most other storms — are accompanied by periods of intensely low barometric pressure. Whitetails tend to roam wide in search of food prior to a storm. But they hole up when snow actually starts to fall. And they stay holed up until the storm passes or at least until it eases off.

It has been revealed that third, while snow means hunters can see deer moving much more easily, it also works the other way around. Deer see the hunter coming a lot farther off. The fact that snow silences the woods forces deer to use their eyes more. Ever spend an hour or two watching a band of deer bedded down after a snowstorm? Their heads are lifted much more often to eyeball the surrounding terrain. Eyes must assume a vigil which ears can no longer accomplish and must provide the essential early warning. Incidentally, your own hearing abilities aren’t helped by snowfall, either. Deer that rustled the crisp frozen leaves of a frosty fall morning won’t be heard walking through a soft cover of new-fallen snow.

Fourth, snow changes whitetail eating habits — particularly heavy snowfall. Meadow grasses may not be pawed at again until spring. Buds, twigs and surviving leafy vegetation take its place. These plants are less nutritious for deer but they are easier to obtain. Waste grains in fields blown clear of snow may promote a concentration of feeding whitetails.

So now you are thinking that snowfall might not be such a boon to hunting?

Actually, it is — if you know how to use it to your advantage.

Whitetails, like all wildlife, are creatures of habit. You can predict a deer’s general reaction to things that impact on its environment. Maybe your predictions won’t be precise but they can be close enough to cut down on the number of fruitless hunting efforts you make.

Recent findings suggest that pay attention to the weatherman. Be sure you are out hunting on the day before a storm is forecast to arrive. Through changes in barometric pressure, deer sense the oncoming storm. They often move out to feed as heavily as possible — even in the middle of the day — forgoing the usual bedding hours in their hasty urge to stock up before the storm. So be sure to hunt all day.

Sources indicate that pre-storm is the time to concentrate on checking food sources for whitetails. Hunting pressure earlier in the season may have forced the animals to visit open grainfields only at night. If hunter numbers have dwindled — as they do in most states after the first four or five days of the season — start checking those fields again at dawn and dusk. The urge to fill up before a storm may have deer less cautious.

In a recent development, in woodland areas, check hidden openings or meadow edges where wild herbaceous cover remains. Don’t overlook timber cuttings where saplings provide cover and the lack of an overstory promotes the undergrowth that deer savor. Try the creek bottoms where frost may not have killed the green grasses yet.

In farmlands, glass the local hay fields or even vegetable patches where potatoes, sugar beets, carrots, turnips or other root-type plants have not all been harvested yet. And visit abandoned orchards where fallen fruit may provide an attraction.

More than once in a late deer season afternoon, while driving the back roads of farm country near where I live, I have become aware of more and more deer suddenly appearing where few were before. The back edge of a cutover hay field will hold five or six deer, all feeding near a heavy hickory and oak woodlot. Harvested cornfields may have a few animals wandering along, plucking up the waste dumped by corn pickers before it can be plowed under.

Does tend to move farther from cover than bucks, particularly when feeding in daylight hours prior to a storm. But expect surprises. Once, while walking across a partially harvested cornfield to reach a gun blind in the woodlot beyond, I stumbled across a fine eight-point buck. This lone deer, feeding in a 12-row patch of standing corn, was fully 80 yards from the nearest heavy cover. He evidently felt safe among the withered cornstalks. And their rattling in the wind had probably masked the sound of my approach.

According to recent reports, I was so startled, in fact, that I never got off a shot from the slug-loaded 12-gauge that I was carrying. The buck wheeled and bounded away before I could shoot.

Don’t be caught unprepared. You never know where a deer will suddenly appear. I’ve had does dart from brushy drainage ditches — deep ones that were mostly dry or had the damp patches frozen solid by late fall’s icy weather. Ditches provide perfect cover routes to reach open stretches with food. Shelterbelts do so, too.

It has been revealed that once a storm of some magnitude starts, deer simply disappear. Whitetails of both sexes will head for the thickest most protective cover around. Conifers are ideal (pine plantations or cedar swamps in the North Country). In farmlands, overgrown brushy woodlots or thick river bottom or creekbottom cover is an alternative. Here deer will lie down and, unless disturbed by a hunter wandering around in the storm, they will not get up for hours — maybe days.

According to recent reports, the hollow hair in deer’s coats provides superb insulation from the snow’s cold and dampness. Curled up into a small oval (judge for yourself how compactly a whitetail can curl up by the sizes of the beds you’ll find a day or so later) deer will ride out the storm, sometimes allowing the snowfall to almost literally cover them. They don’t seek food and they don’t move much — even to stand and stretch.

Recent findings suggest that because hunters don’t normally slog around in heavy storms, deer are usually undisturbed until the snowfall begins to lessen. If a storm lasts more than a day, deer may move around close to their bedding areas but they won’t venture far.

It is an ideal time, once the storm begins to subside, to mount a deer drive.

Pinpointing whitetail cover won’t be difficult, even with the lack of tracks on new-fallen snow. Just pick the heaviest thickest junk around. Match the size of the cover to the number of drivers and standers you have with you, and you should be able to fill several tags for your group.

There is a farmland county near my Michigan home which is a mixture of cedar swamp, brushy woodlots and grainfields, plus some pastureland. Every other season or so, myself and about five of my hunting buddies drive over there on a Saturday. At this time, we’ve all just come back from the North Country’s season opener; perhaps half of us have been fortunate enough to have scored on a buck already. The lucky ones drive for their less successful counterparts.

Through the years, we have secured hunting permission by telephone and by long acquaintance with the local landowners, some of whom join us for these drives. Because this area is open to the use of high-power rifles, it takes only about three or four standers to cover all downwind and sidewind exit routes in the cover we visit.

Recent findings suggest that the remainder of us cast back and forth in a line — more or less — of drivers, working silently in the belief that noise startles deer even more than human scent and sends them into headlong flight. We want the whitetails to break cover in a nervous trot, glancing back over their shoulders, not fleeing at top speed.

It has been revealed that because the drivers move and the deer focus their attention on them, the standers get some easy shots. Standers are urged to find natural blinds that will camouflage just a bit of the brilliance of the Blaze Orange garments they wear.

Drivers wear as much Blaze Orange as possible for high visibility. They don’t carry firearms, either, on our drives.

Such minidrives have proved extremely successful. In those years when we all fill tags up north and don’t proposal to visit this county, local landowners call us to see if we’re coming over to help them. It has become a social event. We do go, of course.

Industry observers note that well-conducted drives, frankly, are one of the best ways to kill whitetails all season long — early or late, in snow or without it. If you develop a compatible group of hunters who are all safety conscious, driving may well be the best way to hunt.

For the single hunter, stillhunting in the snow can prove difficult. The muffling effect snow has on sounds is appealing to stillhunters but they should remember that whitetails bedded in snow can be extremely watchful. That’s true at least while a storm is waning or before the sun reappears with warmth enough to prompt more movement of deer. Whitetails scan their surroundings intently. And because they are not likely to be moving, spotting them will prove that much tougher.

Recent findings suggest that if a stillhunter is extremely patient and slow moving, maybe he has a chance. But the average hunter who enjoys some success stillhunting on bare ground may find snowy days beyond his capability.

There is another factor making things tougher: wind. Snowstorms are often accompanied by high winds, ones that don’t die off when the snow stops falling. Wind makes all wildlife nervous. Their hearing isn’t as useful. Add that problem to the noise-muffling effect snow already has and you come up with doubly watchful whitetails.

According to recent reports, so what about doing what you sometimes hear old-timers describe? Just plant yourself on a massive buck’s track and walk him into the ground.

Unless you are a true woodsman, which most of us have neither the time nor the inclination to be, forget it. It sounds rather romantic, as the old sporting books told it, but the method isn’t likely to be very rewarding for the hunter of average skill. Oh, it can be done. And every so often you could be lucky enough to actually walk up on a buck — if you can first figure out which tracks belong to bucks and which belong to does. No, the average lone hunter faced with a snowstorm is better off doing just what the deer do: Wait it out.

Once the storm passes, whitetails will begin to circulate once again. Hunger drives them from their beds but sunny weather after a storm seems to invigorate deer, too. No scientific facts back up this phenomenon and I claim no insight into the psychology of deer. It’s just a gut feeling I have about whitetails based on observations of the ways yearlings almost cavort after a storm passes. Young bucks, not part of the serious breeding process that is probably about over when snow begins to fall, seem to want to spar. They push each other around rather good naturedly. The older does concentrate on finding food. Now’s the time for the smart single hunter to be on his stand or in his blind.

Recent findings suggest that surprisingly, there’s little need to hurry in the morning, either. Deer must feel the cold to some degree because they seldom stir at the crack of dawn after a very cold night. That fact doesn’t mean a hunter shouldn’t be out before daybreak — as he would be earlier in the season. Some whitetails may be stirring. But many times after a storm I’ve witnessed deer waiting until the sun was shining full upon them, waiting for an hour or more after daylight, before moving out to feed. It’s as if they were lying there, soaking up the warmth of the sun.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, deer will often be feeding — or moving to and from feeding areas — in the middle of the day after the return of good weather conditions. For the man in a blind, deer moving on snow in full daylight are easy to spot.

Sources indicate that remember, also, that bedding areas on southern exposures — places where the effects of the warm sun are felt the most intensely — will be favored by deer. Anytime the temperature is under 35°, deer seem to prefer places where the sun can hit them in the morning. If it is out of prevailing winds, so much the better.

According to recent reports, unlike the majority of Western mule deer, which must move from higher mountain summer range to the valleys each winter, whitetails normally find everything they need to survive in a year-round home. One exception is Michigan’s Upper Peninsula where deer summering in the Lake Superior watershed tend to wander southward toward the more temperate climate of Lake Michigan in late fall and early winter, often before deer season ends. Snowfall prompts even greater movement.

A few of these whitetails travel quite a distance — 40 or maybe 50 miles. Some don’t move at all but take their chances in the deeper snowfall and reduced winter food conditions of the northern watershed. If you are aware of such a migration where you hunt, take advantage of it. The routes traveled are not always as predictable as the game trails muleys use to move downhill but various general routes are used year after year. Spot blinds accordingly.

According to recent reports, the best advice for winter stand hunting, I think, is to stay put and to stay as comfortable as possible. Dress to remain warm in below-freezing temperatures. Make sure that your blind is well situated and that it is constructed in such a way that it blocks out any stray winds. Get a back rest and sit on a patch of canvas or plastic to keep the snow from soaking through.

I always make sure that I have a Thermos of hot coffee, tea or cocoa handy. A blind means you can move around a little without being seen and a few gulps of warm liquid can brighten a dreary day.

Industry observers note that and be patient. Deer won’t move as often or as far in snowy weather — unless it’s a bright warm day with temperatures rising above freezing. If you are hunting alone, be prepared to wait them out. And do it in a place where they’re likely to be: near a food source or along (or in the midst of) the heavier cover where they’re certain to bed down.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

According to recent reports, winter hunting doesn’t have to be a case of survival against the elements. You can be comfortable and successful and see more than just tracks.

This story, “Snowstorm Whitetails,” appeared in the December 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.

#216775. The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4517 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when I was a skinny, major-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family.
  • Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.
  • Industry observers note that on the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when I was a skinny, major-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family. Nowadays, thanks to the game commission’s deer stocking and management programs, deer are plentiful in the mountains of east Tennessee, but in the 1940s they were nonexistent. That meant that going on a real deer hunt involved traveling hundreds of miles and visiting places as far removed from our farm as was the back side of the moon. It was, to my mind, an elegant adventure, sort of like going to Europe or taking an ocean cruise. Nothing could be finer. My chums were green with envy.

Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.

Industry observers note that on the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse. I remember inspecting the animal in elaborate detail; feeling the texture of its hair, looking at its teeth and bones and, most of all, marveling at the wonder of its gracefully curved antlers.

Recent findings suggest that horns, as they grew on cows and bulls, were familiar to me. But antlers were something entirely different — harder, more graceful and certainly more dangerous looking. I nearly lost my senses when told they were shed and regrown every year. For a while I simply didn’t believe it and only gradually allowed myself to be convinced.

Recent findings suggest that and deer could jump, too, higher than a cow or even a horse. My imagination reeled with stories of these wonderful animals.

“Come on,” I remarked, “nothing can jump a high-wire fence.” So my host took me to a crossing place and showed where the deer-tracked path led up to a fence then continued on the other side. “Wow, they really can do it. Wait till I tell Mom.”.

Next day, after breakfast of deer loin, rich gravy and biscuits, I stood in front of the gun rack, itching to get my hands on a genuine deer rifle and go hunting for these wonderful animals. Already, visions of great stags were dancing through my head.

My dad took the first rifle, a Model 99 Savage in .250 caliber, and my brother selected a shortened .30/40 Krag. Why, I wondered, had he passed over a truly beautiful Model 141 Remington pump-action rifle in .30 Remington in favor of the Krag? Anyway, I liked the pump and was glad I had a chance to use it. But when I was clear of the barn lot and stopped to load the rifle, his motives became clear. Nearly all of the cartridges had a sharp indentation on the primer, meaning they had previously misfired and were now useless. Of the lot, only three had virgin primers, and these I fed into the rifle with the optimism of youth.

Less than an hour later, I “jumped” a deer literally in his bed. He came up so close to me that for a moment I was so startled I almost turned and ran. He was not the stag of my dreams but he did have antlers, perhaps six points, and he could be mine! At first the buck ran away so fast that it looked as though I wouldn’t have time for a shot, but then he did something that still has me wondering. After running dead away for about 100 yards, he spun around and headed right at me. Clearly, he would pass by within a few feet, and even at full tilt I’d have a fairly easy shot.

Closer he came and the rifle was at my shoulder, my teeth clinched against the fearful recoil, eye squinted over the sights.

“There he is, pull the trigger!”.

According to recent reports, “Hurry, he’s getting away. Try another shot!”.

Then the buck whirled again and headed back at me again! He was passing by close enough to hit with a hoe handle.

In a recent development, tears streamed down my cheeks. Tears of disappointment, tears of frustration and tears of anger. I’d had a better than fair chance and lost it because of grown-ups who’d palmed off a bunch of useless cartridges on me. On the way back to the house, I tried the last cartridge but like its brethren, it only clicked in dismal failure.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

As it turned out, I was the only hunter who’d had a “shot” that day, meaning that on the following morning the gun rack was again emptied of all workable deer rifles. All that was left was a little Mossberg Model 151 Rimfire Autoloader complete with a 4X scope (don’t ask how I remember these details, how could I possibly forget?) and several boxes of Super-X ammo.

Sources indicate that the day before, I’d passed a newly disked and seeded field of winter wheat that was covered with crows. Surely they would be there again. “If I can’t shoot a deer, at least I’ll shoot some crows,” I told myself as I lifted the .22 from the rack and pocketed a box of ammo.

The crows were there, within easy range, but my first shot kicked up dust far to the left and lower than where I’d aimed. When the crows settled back I missed again the same way. Clearly the rifle didn’t hit where the scope aimed. Why? The rest of the day, and the days following, were spent unraveling the mysteries of sight adjustment and bullet trajectory. A whole newly introduced world of excitement lay before me. So many things to learn about guns and only a lifetime to study them.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

A small boy can do worse than go deer hunting, even with a rifle that won’t work.

Every time I look at the 12-point whitetail mounted on my trophy room wall, I wonder if I’d do it over again if I had the chance.

Sources indicate that it was December ’77 and I was after major whitetails on the Guajolota (translates to female turkey) Ranch in deep south Texas. When I say big whitetails, I don’t mean just big, but big-big, Texas-big, the kind of big that makes vaqueros (cowboys) whisper “muy grande” in wide-eyed wonder. The Guajolota is a working cow ranch but, like most big spreads in south Texas, it swarms with quail and so many big-antlered whitetails that owner Jim McAllen got the idea that he could make more money “farming” deer than beef.

Sources indicate that so true to his stock-breeding tradition (McAllen, Texas, is named after Jim’s pioneer family), he set out to make his herd of deer bigger and better by using the same selective breeding techniques proven in the development of superior beef herds. In Texas, just about everyone who hunts deer either owns land, leases hunting rights or hunts on a “pay per day” ranch. (That “per day” arrangement is not the same sort of operation as the exotic game ranches, which also flourish in Texas.) Accordingly, McAllen figured that if he could breed a “super” race of elk-headed whitetails, hunters would just naturally pay more to hunt on the Guajolota.

Recent findings suggest that the first step in his program was to kill off the “culls” — bucks with skimpy antlers and a tendency to pass on this trait — and save the giant bucks for a while for breeding. The program had been in effect only a few years when I hunted the Guajolota, but signs of its success were abundant on my first morning of hunting.

Accompanied by my pal Jim Nolen, maker of the well-known Nolen knives and guided by Ed Dutch, who at that time was the ranch’s game biologist but has since become a top wildlife photographer, we hid under a mesquite tree where we could look out over a 60-yard flat of open grassland.

With a bit of imagination, you might call the south Texas terrain “brush country,” but it’s not the kind of brush hunting one gets in, say, Pennsylvania or Missouri. Just about everything that grows wild in that part of the Texas empire either sticks, scratches bites or poisons, so stalking deer through the cactus and catclaw isn’t all that much fun. That’s why hunting is usually done from a quick stand or from a high seat that lets you look over the thorny chaparral. Fortunately, there is a high buck-to-doe ratio that makes the bucks especially aggressive and eager to challenge other bucks for available does.

It has been revealed that the sound of these bucks doing battle is a distinctive clicking and rubbing of antlers that can be heard a pretty fair ways and has the effect of calling other bucks to join the fray. If you ever happen to come upon a couple of bucks fighting it out over some does, you’ll probably spot one or two more waiting their turn, and while the fighting is going on, a smarter-than-average Romeo may be trying to make off with the harem.

Many years ago, some deer hunters had the clever idea of banging a couple of deer antlers together to imitate the sounds of a fight and thereby call bucks to the gun. It worked like a charm and “rattling” up bucks has become an accepted form of the hunting arts.

It has been revealed that I’ve tried rattling bucks from Maine to California but the only places I’ve had much success were in areas of dense deer population where there were plenty of aggressive bucks. South Texas is the home of rattling, with both the terrain and temperament of the bucks ideally suited for the technique. The trick, though, in addition to knowing how to rattle the antlers together, is finding a stand that gives you a fairly good view of at least an acre or so of relatively open space.

It has been revealed that some bucks apparently lose all reason at the sound of a fight and dash right in where at any other season they would fear to tread. Some rattlers report having snorting bucks right in their laps after only a moment or two of clicking the antlers. Wiser bucks will come in more cautiously, perhaps circling the stand, wanting to get sight or wind of the combatants. Thus, if you position yourself on the edge of a clearing, you get to see the deer before he gets too close. This also gives the deer a bit of breathing room so he won’t have to get too close and overly spooky. You’ll see deer heads poking out of the bush around the clearing, ears forward, and too curious — or determined — to bound away. More often than not, there’s time for a well-aimed shot, but be sure to keep your rifle close to your shoulder and ready to fire. If they see you move, they’re gone in a flash. Man, deer or fowl, there’s something about poaching on another’s territory that makes any male more than a little spooky.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed.

I settled back against the forked trunk of the mesquite tree with my rifle resting on my knees. It was a trim little .250/3000 bolt gun stocked by Don Allen and built on a Mauser action that had been shortened a full inch by ace metalsmith Ron Lampert. Nolen, who was to take first turn playing the antlers, was just to my right and Dutch, who wanted some pictures, was a few yards behind, manning a telephoto lens.

Results were almost immediate. Nolen had banged the antlers no more than twice, twisting and rubbing them together to make the characteristic scrape-click-scrape sound of fighting deer when there, right in front of me, snorting and stomping his feet, was the biggest whitetail buck I’d ever seen on the hoof. He was huge, with perfectly symmetrical antlers. The main beams seemed to grow straight out in a horizontal line before hooking in at the tips. His points stood straight up like rods in an iron gate and the whole picture was a deer-hunter’s fantasy. The buck of a lifetime, too substantial to be true, perfect. It had to be a lie, a tale told in a deer camp, vividly remembered.

Recent findings suggest that but he was there, stomping, snorting, beautiful. All I had to do was put the crosshairs on his chest and touch the trigger and my whitetail-hunting days would be over, for never would I see a bigger buck. For long moments, I held the crosshairs on his chest, poised to shoot, listening for the click of Dutch’s camera, Click-click-click it went. Now I had a record of the moment, a deer hunter at the gates of paradise. Every nerve in me howled “pull the trigger, pull the trigger,” but I didn’t.

It has been revealed that greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed. “Look old boy,” it mentioned to me, “this is only the first deer. Think about the really massive ones that are waiting back there in the thicket. We’ve got lots of time to wait for the absolute world beater.”.

Incredibly, I lowered my rifle, worked the bolt and emptied the chamber. Then, settling the crosshairs back on the buck’s chest, I tickled the trigger.

“Click,” it went, and the buck was gone.

“Just wanted to know what it felt like to pull the trigger on a giant buck,” I explained to an absolutely astonished Jim Nolen.

“Why didn’t you shoot?” Dutch asked.

“Waiting for something bigger,” I allowed.

“That’s as big as they get,” was his answer, and I knew greed had done me in.

That morning we rattled in a couple more trophy-size bucks, but nothing nearly so grand as the first, so I couldn’t bring myself to raise the rifle. That afternoon, after a lunch of chili and frijoles served on a tortilla, cowboy-style, followed by a siesta, we tried again — but the antlers were cold and nothing answered the challenge.

It has been revealed that that evening a few of McAllen’s vaqueros stopped by the bunkhouse for cerveza and conversation. “It is true,” they asked, “you had El Macho Grande in your sights and did not shoot? Why?”.

I really couldn’t answer, but one thing for sure, if I ever saw him again I would shoot.

Next day the antlers were still cold, so by midafternoon we changed tactics and climbed into a tower where we could watch for deer crossing a narrow sendero (a rough, clear-cut roadway). The view from the tower allowed us to look down into the endless thicket, but no deer were moving. By early evening I had counted dozens of javelina, the small wild pigs of the Southwest, and had seen more quail than I thought existed, but no deer other than an occasional doe.

Industry observers note that the sun hung low over the deep Texas thicket and a soft haze had wrapped itself around the evening air when the buck stepped into the sendero. The distance was just a bit more than 200 yards, but even with my 7X binoculars, the antlers were hard to judge because the sun was behind the deer, reflecting through the haze so that the deer seemed to be the center of a psychedelic burst of rainbow color. It was not a vision of earth, but a dream in pastel colors with quail calls for background music.

The buck moved slowly, a step at a time, nibbling shoots of greenery. But his antlers remained a mystery. We could see that they were big and exceptionally high, but the way they reflected shafts of gilded light made rational judgment impossible.

“I can’t see his antlers clearly,” Nolen whispered, “but I can see points everywhere.”.

Industry observers note that the buck was nearly across the sendero now and in a moment he would be gone, perhaps forever. I’d already let the trophy of a lifetime slip through my fingers. Did I dare risk losing a second chance? My trigger finger tightened and the little rifle spoke gently to the soft evening.

The buck was a freak, wearing incredible antlers that had grown to typical, though huge, shape on the right side but with an oddly palmated branch on the left. Is it the trophy of a lifetime, a one-of-a-kind specimen never to be duplicated? Or just a freak with outsize antler growth? I wonder. I wonder every time I look at it on the wall.

Industry observers note that in addition to liberal season and bag limits, Alabama has some of the biggest-antlered and heaviest-bodied whitetails I’ve ever looked at. One Alabama trophy deer I saw a few years back got me so excited that I spent several consecutive seasons there trying to bring home the granddaddy.

Sources indicate that and I saw lots of bucks, some eight and 10-pointers with such seductive racks that I was often tempted to touch the trigger. Patience prevailed, though, and as days turned to weeks I became more or less accustomed to the sight of the Alabama sun setting over a hardwood thicket in which, from a tree stand, I might be glassing from two to six major-antlered bucks at one time. But as I said, I wanted only the he-coon of the hardwoods and nothing else would do.

How was it, then, that I eventually shot a little eight-pointer?

It has been revealed that hoping to relieve the tedium of my daily wait-and-watch routine, I got myself invited to a party hunt, and on the appointed morning found myself in the midst of an incredible spectacle. The setting was a beautiful Southern mansion complete with curving driveway and vast, oak-bordered lawns. What made the scene so bizarre was the unbelievable variety of humanity strolling or squatting about the neatly clipped grounds. Tweed shooting jackets and English riding boots mixed with faded overalls and run-down clodhoppers while the elegant accents of aristocratic Southern speech were punctuated with the staccato “patoos” of well-aimed tobacco juice. There had been a violent thunderstorm during the night, and judging by the smells of wet wool and soaked leather, many of the attendees had passed the night in the rain.

In a recent development, A metal tub about the size of a horse watering trough was being set up on a stone foundation, eventually to be filled with gallons of cooking oil, and nearby a wild-eyed chap was tugging at a heavy chain leash in a futile attempt to separate two snarling dogs. “Get back,” he yelled when I approached to help, “these dogs are killers.”.

“Then why don’t you leave them alone?” I asked.

“I’m trying to keep them from killing each other until Big Bob wakes up.”.

“Who is Big Bob?” I had to ask.

“That’s him over yonder,” he responded, waving his free hand in the direction of an inert form stretched out in the tangled remains of what appeared to have once been a rose garden.

I meant to take a closer look, but at that moment a silence fell over the assembly as a spry black man of uncertain vintage, his hair a fluffy white, came down the brick-paved path leading from the significant house.

According to recent reports, “Mista William is a commin’,” he chanted. “Mista William is commin’, here he come now.”.

Sure enough, there was the great one himself, Mister William, owner of thousands of acres of prime farmland and hardwoods, home to the biggest whitetails to be found anywhere. Obviously, Mister William had reached that unique station in society where elegant or even proper attire was no longer required as an emblem of station or success. Accordingly, he was outfitted in soiled chino work pants and shirt, the tail of the latter flapping loosely about his backside, muddied work shoes with, as I remember, only one sock and crowned off with an ancient straw hat that was liberally ventilated with odd-size holes. Yet there was no denying his regal presence. As he puffed unsteadily along the brick pavement, pausing occasionally to scratch, spit or realign his direction, there was a chorus of salutations and more than a few caps were doffed.

“Mornin’ Mista William.” “Fine day Bill.” “Good to see you Mista Bill.”.

Each greeting was received with a wave and every face was recognized by name.

Recent findings suggest that “Glad to see you, Jack.” “Nice of you to come over, Pete. How’s Mary and the kids?” “Hi Ralph.”.

When at last he faced me, his eyes narrowed, searching for a name.

“Nice to meet you sir. I’m Jim Carmichel and I appreciated the invitation to your deer hunt.”.

“Glad to have you, glad to have you,” he gestured grandly. “This hunt ain’t much, just something me and the boys like to do every year about this time.

Industry observers note that “Hey there you, Jake, tell Big Bob I stated to put Mr. Carmichel here on the road where the deer cross.”.

Sources indicate that with that he ambled back up the walk, mounted the porch steps and turned to face the breathless assembly. “Boys, the hunt’s on.”.

According to recent reports, the next few moments were lost in a bedlam of shouts, cheers, running feet and spinning truck tires. Seated in the back of a pickup (I almost made the fatal mistake of climbing into a truck full of savage curs) that fishtailed out of the driveway in a shower of mud and gravel, I caught a glimpse of Mister William as he turned and re-entered the great house, aided by his white-topped butler. Apparently he was not attending his own hunt.

Positioned as I was, on a muddied logging road, I could hear the baying pack of Catahoula curs as they topped a ridge nearly a mile away. As the baying grew louder, it was apparent they were coming my way and would cross the road in front of me. Mister William had indeed given me the best stand on the hunt and in just a few moments I would have a shot.

According to recent reports, I was using a borrowed shotgun loaded with No. 000 buckshot and the deer would be crossing from right to left, a dead-easy setup. When the deer broke from cover and bounded across the road, I swung the bead some two feet ahead of his chest and was tightening on the trigger when I realized that it wasn’t much of a buck. An eight-pointer, perhaps, but it was a bucket-head without much width, height, or thickness of beam. The buck certainly wasn’t the world-beater I wanted. With another bound, the young buck disappeared into more timber.

By then the road was covered by a blanket of howling and snarling beasts with their owner, Big Bob, not far behind.

This was the first time I had had a close-up look at Substantial Bob and he was, to be sure, an awesome apparition. Clad only in bib overalls and a white T-shirt, despite the chill of the day, Big Bob stood a good six or eight inches over six feet and was as wide as a church door. His hair, probably waist length, was knotted behind his head in the style of a samurai warrior, and when he spoke I could see that every tooth in his head was covered in gold. His bout with the rose garden had criss-crossed his arms and face with bloody lacerations, and at his side swung a hunting knife that looked as long as a Saracen scimitar.

As he strode toward me — eyes wild, face blood-caked and mouth flashing of gold — the sword banged against his knee. It was the only weapon he carried. Considering his size, the obvious strength of his hands and arms and the fierceness of his countenance, the knife was more of an affectation than a necessity.

In a recent development, “Where’s the deer?” he asked. “I didn’t hear you shoot.”.

In a recent development, “How come? His tracks is right there in front of you.”.

“He wasn’t a good trophy,” I answered.

At this, his eyes narrowed, “Mister, we ain’t huntin’ trophies, we’re huntin’ meat. We got a lot of people to feed tonight and if you don’t shoot somethin’ these dogs get meaner than they already are.” Significant Bob made his point very convincingly.

“The next time something comes by, I’ll be sure to shoot,” I promised.

And that’s exactly what I did. A couple of hours later, the howling pack came by again in violent pursuit of a distinctly undistinguished little eight-pointer.

That evening, my buck and two others that had been killed during the hunt were sliced into bite-size chunks, rolled in batter and deep-fried in the gas-fired horse trough I’d noted earlier.

In a recent development, in time, huge platters were stacked with the delicious-smelling venison tidbits but, for some reason, no one took so much as a single bite. This struck me as curious because no one had eaten since breakfast and I assumed that everyone was as famished as I was. Not wanting to violate local custom, I decided it best not to serve myself until someone else had done so.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for the holdup was soon apparent, however, when Mister William’s butler appeared and announced the immediate arrival of his benefactor. “Here come Mista William, ever’body git ready, here he come now.”.

Mister William’s appearance was greatly improved; not only was he better turned out than several hours previous, but his gait was markedly steadier.

Without a word to the hushed onlookers, he marched straight to the deep-fry trough and extracted a crispy brown morsel of batter-dipped venison. For a moment he chewed thoughtfully, eyes cast heavenward. Then, with a sly smile, he made his pronouncement, “Boys, this meat is fit to eat.”.

Later, food and drink in hand, I was buttonholed by Massive Bob, his countenance no less ominous than earlier and his face still blood-caked from his personal war of the roses.

“If you had shot that other deer,” he allowed, “we would have had some extra meat for my dogs. Now I have to feed ’em dry dog food, which makes their bowels tight and they get meaner than ever.”.

“Here,” I answered, handing him my half-emptied plate, “they can have mine.”.

This story, “Whitetails I Have Known,” appeared in the September 1982 problem of Outdoor Life.

10 Ski Run Drop-Ins That Require Serious Nerve

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every expert skier knows this feeling: You’re standing at the top of a run, skis pointed downhill, looking over an entrance that suddenly seems a whole lot steeper than it did from the lift.
  • Whatever the obstacle, some ski runs are intimidating before you even make your first turn.
  • *Conditions and snow depth greatly affect how skiable the following runs are at any given time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Jackson Hole).

Sources indicate that every expert skier knows this feeling: You’re standing at the top of a run, skis pointed downhill, looking over an entrance that suddenly seems a whole lot steeper than it did from the lift. Maybe there’s a cornice to negotiate, a narrow rock-lined chute to squeeze through, or a cliff that requires a leap of faith. The remainder of the run beyond the drop-in might be flat, for all you know, but getting to it is the challenge of the day.

Whatever the obstacle, some ski runs are intimidating before you even make your first turn. From legendary big-mountain lines to tight, technical chutes, these 10 North American drop-ins are guaranteed to get your heart pumping. Consider them inspiration for the season ahead—or a reminder that sometimes it’s perfectly fine to admire the view from above.

*Conditions and snow depth greatly affect how skiable the following runs are at any given time. Check trail status and heed all warnings and closures before dropping in.

It’s hard to make a list like this without kicking it off with Corbet’s. Perhaps the most famous—and most photographed—ski entrance in North America, this Jackson Hole icon requires skiers to negotiate a rocky cornice before dropping roughly 10 to 20 feet into a narrow, steep couloir. The landing can be soft powder or unforgiving hardpack, depending on conditions, and there’s often a crowd gathered above to watch the action. No pressure. There’s even an entire event dedicated to how stylish—or catastrophic—skiers navigate this tricky entrance.

Recent findings suggest that think Corbet’s is intimidating? Meet its even scarierl next-door neighbor. Located just skier’s left of Corbet’s, S&S features a mandatory cliff drop of up to 25 feet, followed by a tight landing and a narrow couloir. Skiers need to make a midair adjustment to line up the landing, leaving little room for error. This one is strictly for the seriously experienced.

According to recent reports, the name doesn’t undersell it. Massive Sky’s legendary Big Couloir begins with an exposed, rocky entrance that can involve negotiating a cornice before dropping into a narrow, sustained chute. With pitches approaching 50 degrees and a 1,400-foot descent below, it’s a serious commitment from the first turn. Access is controlled by ski patrol, and skiers must check in and carry avalanche safety equipment.

Sources indicate that alyeska doesn’t do subtle when it comes to steep terrain, and Christmas Chute is a perfect example. The entrance funnels skiers between imposing rock walls before opening into a steep, confined chute. The line averages roughly 45 degrees and drops about 1,500 vertical feet. It’s an intimidating entrance in a spectacularly Alaskan setting, where the mountains are massive and the consequences are real.

Sources indicate that even the name is enough to make you think twice. The Coffin is a notorious narrow passage in Whistler’s alpine terrain, where skiers squeeze through a tight, rock-lined opening before dropping into the terrain below. Visible from the Peak Chair—but not officially on the trail map—it’s also a popular spectator attraction. The confined entrance leaves little room to get comfortable, making the moment you drop in particularly memorable.

Palisades Tahoe has no shortage of intimidating terrain, but McConkey’s is among its signature tests of nerve. This steep, rocky feature demands commitment from the entrance, with exposed terrain and little margin for error. The line’s reputation is part of what makes it so compelling: Even accomplished skiers may take a long look before deciding whether today’s the day.

Not every intimidating entrance involves a giant cliff or mandatory air. Sometimes it’s what you can’t see that gets the adrenaline going. Lobotomy, located off of Silver King peak, in Crystal’s sidecounty zone, is known for its blind entrance and consequential no-fall-zone skiing. You can’t simply peer over the edge and map out every turn before committing. It’s a different kind of mental challenge, and one that earns this line a spot on the list. Note that this is technically hike-to terrain, so come prepared with all the necessary equipment.

Snowbird is for its steep skiing, and Pipeline Couloir is one of its more intimidating challenges. Getting there requires a hike, but the real test begins when skiers reach the entrance: a steep, rocky drop-in that demands solid technical skills before the couloir even opens up. It’s a reminder that sometimes the most intimidating part of a massive-mountain line isn’t the descent itself, but getting those first few turns just right.

Revelstoke is a playground for skiers who like their terrain steep, deep, and a little intimidating. With a technical entrance and steep, demanding terrain, Discipline rewards, well, discipline and confident, precise skiing. Depending on conditions, the entrance can feature a cornice that adds another layer of commitment.

In a recent development, the East Coast gets in on the fun with this Mad River Glen adventure. Paradise is an all-natural trail that starts with a steep drop-in before winding through tight trees, bumps, and rugged New England terrain. There’s no wide-open groomed runway here, and the entrance sets the tone for all that follows. Paradise offers a totally different vibe than all the others on this list, but it’s no less intimidating for those who dare.

Breaking: Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Recent findings suggest that some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

According to recent reports, however, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Recent findings suggest that unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern Upcoming Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the Fresh Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Sources indicate that crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

According to recent reports, why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

Industry observers note that one of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Sources indicate that perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

According to recent reports, winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

According to recent reports, desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

In a recent development, on long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries swiftly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

#216769. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (865 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Recent findings suggest that there is a cinema up north.
  • In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

Recent findings suggest that there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

This is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

Sources indicate that but can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

In a recent development, I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

However, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a major-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

It has been revealed that my reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

Recent findings suggest that I watched The Alpinist on the big screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

Industry observers note that but anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

Recent findings suggest that from my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

World Cup Ski Racing Is Back in Colorado. Here’s Who—and How—to Watch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Cochran-Siegle at Copper Media Days on November 18, 2026 at Copper Mountain Resort in Copper Mountain, Colorado.
  • World Cup skiing returns to Colorado this weekend as Copper Mountain hosts the Stifel Copper Cup for two days of high-speed competition.
  • 28-29 event features men’s super-G on Saturday and giant slalom on Sunday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ryan Cochran-Siegle at Copper Media Days on November 18, 2026 at Copper Mountain Resort in Copper Mountain, Colorado. Photo: @dustinsatloff // @usskiteam (Photo: Dustin Satloff).

World Cup skiing returns to Colorado this weekend as Copper Mountain hosts the Stifel Copper Cup for two days of high-speed competition. For American fans, it’s a chance to cheer on the U.S. Ski Team on familiar terrain—and to see how the country’s top male skiers stack up against a formidable international field.

The Nov. 28-29 event features men’s super-G on Saturday and giant slalom on Sunday. Saturday’s race is particularly noteworthy: It marks the first men’s speed race of the 2026-’27 World Cup season and the first domestic men’s World Cup stop of the winter.

And while the international field is loaded with star power, including Swiss superstar Marco Odermatt, there are several Americans worth keeping an eye on this weekend.

Industry observers note that the headliner for the American men is Vermont native Ryan Cochran-Siegle, a two-time Olympic silver medalist in super-G and one of the country’s most accomplished speed specialists. He’ll make his season debut Saturday in a discipline where he’s proven he can hang with the very best.

In a recent development, cochran-Siegle earned silver in super-G at the 2022 Beijing Olympics and added another silver in the team combined at the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Games. He’s also a former World Cup super-G winner, and his combination of technical prowess and comfort at high speeds makes him America’s best shot at a podium on Saturday.

It’s worth noting that Copper’s super-G marks the first men’s speed race of the season, meaning everyone is starting from scratch in the discipline. Cochran-Siegle will have the home-country crowd behind him as he takes on a field led by Odermatt and reigning Olympic super-G champion Franjo von Allmen, both of Switzerland.

For Colorado ski fans, River Radamus’ name always elicits excitement. The Edwards native grew up skiing at Vail, where his parents were ski coaches, and has become one of the most consistent American giant slalom racers on the World Cup circuit.

According to recent reports, radamus, known for his aggressive skiing style, has developed into a regular World Cup points scorer and a legitimate contender when the course suits his strengths. He’s also familiar with Copper’s terrain from years of training at the resort.

Sunday’s giant slalom will be a particularly tough test, with Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic GS champion and Crystal Globe winner, leading the field. Odermatt and Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard are also contenders to watch.

According to recent reports, another Colorado connection is Kyle Negomir, a Littleton native and Ski & Snowboard Club Vail product who represents the next wave of American men’s racing. Negomir competes in the technical and speed disciplines and has been working to establish himself as a consistent World Cup presence.

In a recent development, with the American men looking to build depth behind established veterans like Cochran-Siegle, Negomir is one to watch as the season progresses. A strong showing on home snow would be a significant step forward.

Recent findings suggest that both men’s races stream live on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s super-G coverage begins at 1:45 p.m. ET, and Sunday’s giant slalom starts at noon ET, with the second run at 3 p.m. ET. Spectators can watch in person; general admission is free.
